claims.title: The rock art of Gobustan
claims.summary: On a plateau south of Baku, prehistoric peoples carved more than 6,000 engravings of hunters, animals and boats, leaving a record of roughly 40,000 years of human activity later inscribed by UNESCO.

claims.title: The kingdom of Caucasian Albania
claims.summary: The Caucasian Albanians established a kingdom in the eastern Caucasus, much of which overlaps present-day Azerbaijan, before falling under the suzerainty of the Sasanian Persian Empire.

claims.title: Caucasian Albania adopts Christianity
claims.summary: King Urnayr made Christianity the state religion of Caucasian Albania, which kept its own church and alphabet as a Sasanian province until the Arab conquests.

sources.label: Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia: Country Studies (ed. Glenn E. Curtis)

claims.title: Arab conquest and the coming of Islam
claims.summary: Arab armies brought the eastern Caucasus under Muslim rule, introducing Islam in the seventh century and beginning some four centuries of Arab control over the region.

sources.label: Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia: Country Studies (ed. Glenn E. Curtis)
sources.publisher: Library of Congress, Federal Research Division

claims.title: Seljuk invasions and Turkic settlement
claims.summary: The Seljuk Turks invaded the Caucasus, changing the population and establishing the dominance of Oghuz Turkic, the basis of the modern Azerbaijani language.

claims.title: The Shirvanshahs make Baku their capital
claims.summary: The Shirvanshahs, who had held Baku since the 11th century, made it their capital, walling the inner city and raising the Maiden Tower.

claims.title: The Palace of the Shirvanshahs
claims.summary: The Shirvanshahs built their palace complex in Baku's inner city — reception hall, mosque, mausoleum and bath-house — later inscribed with the walled city by UNESCO in 2000.

claims.title: Ismail I and the Safavid empire
claims.summary: Crowned shah at Tabriz with his base in Azerbaijan, Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty and made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, binding the land to Persia.
claims.citation: Terralore, "The Chronicle of Azerbaijan: From the fire-altars of Caucasian Albania and the Shirvanshahs' Baku to the oil boom, the 1918 republic, Soviet rule and renewed independence.", terralore.co/country/AZE/chronicle#ev-1501-ismail-i-and-the-safavid-empire, claim TL:AZE:event:1501:ismail-i-and-the-safavid-empire, retrieved <YYYY-MM-DD>.

claims.title: Treaty of Gulistan
claims.summary: Ending the Russo-Persian war of 1804–13, Persia ceded to Russia the eastern Caucasus khanates from Lankaran to Derbent, including Baku, Shirvan, Ganja and Karabakh.

claims.title: Treaty of Turkmenchay
claims.summary: The second Russo-Persian war ended with Turkmenchay, confirming Russian rule and adding Nakhichevan and Yerevan, fixing the Aras-river border that still divides the two Azerbaijans.

sources.label: Azerbaijan: Russian suzerainty and the road to independence

claims.title: The Baku oil boom begins
claims.summary: Modern commercial oil extraction began in Baku in 1872; by 1900 the Abşeron field was the largest in the world, turning the city into a global energy capital.

claims.title: Azerbaijan Democratic Republic declared
claims.summary: On 28 May 1918 Azerbaijan declared independence under Musavat leadership, founding the first secular parliamentary republic in the Muslim world, with Mammad Amin Rasulzade among its leaders.

claims.title: Soviet annexation
claims.summary: The Red Army entered Baku in April 1920 against little resistance, ending the democratic republic and bringing Azerbaijan under Soviet rule.

claims.title: Azerbaijan SSR established
claims.summary: Following the Red Army's entry into Baku, the Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republic was formed, becoming a full union republic of the USSR from 1936.

claims.title: Nagorno-Karabakh autonomous oblast created
claims.summary: The Armenian-majority mountainous region of Nagorno-Karabakh was constituted as an autonomous oblast within Soviet Azerbaijan, freezing a contested status that would later erupt.

sources.publisher: Library of Congress, Federal Research Division

claims.title: Karabakh dispute reignites
claims.summary: Under perestroika, Nagorno-Karabakh's Armenian majority demonstrated for transfer to Armenia, triggering intercommunal violence that grew into open conflict as the Soviet Union collapsed.

claims.title: Azerbaijan declares sovereignty
claims.summary: Azerbaijan declared its sovereignty in 1989 as Soviet authority weakened, a first step toward the restoration of independence two years later.

claims.summary: Azerbaijan adopted the Constitutional Act on State Independence, declaring itself successor to the 1918 republic; the US recognised it on 25 December 1991.

claims.title: First Karabakh war ends in ceasefire
claims.summary: A 1994 ceasefire halted the first Nagorno-Karabakh war, leaving Armenian forces in de facto control of the region and surrounding districts, with large displacement on both sides (figures are estimates).

claims.title: Ilham Aliyev succeeds his father
claims.summary: On the death of the gravely ill Heydar Aliyev, his son Ilham Aliyev became president, continuing a family-led order built on Caspian oil and gas wealth.

claims.title: Second Nagorno-Karabakh war
claims.summary: In a 44-day war Azerbaijani forces retook much of Nagorno-Karabakh, capturing Shusha before a ceasefire on 9 November 2020; casualty figures are estimates.

claims.title: Azerbaijan takes full control of Nagorno-Karabakh
claims.summary: A September 2023 offensive brought all of Nagorno-Karabakh under Azerbaijani control and dissolved the self-declared republic; by estimates over 100,000 of about 120,000 ethnic Armenians fled.
